q: Which artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord?
o: The anterior spinal artery (from the vertebral arteries)
why: The single anterior spinal artery (from the vertebrals) supplies the anterior two-thirds; two posterior spinal arteries supply the posterior third. The artery of Adamkiewicz is an important radicular feeder (T9–L2).

q: After anterior cervical discectomy the patient has a hoarse voice. What is the most likely cause?
o: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury from retraction against the ETT cuff
Vocal cord granuloma from the tube
why: Retraction compresses the recurrent laryngeal nerve against the ETT cuff, causing vocal cord palsy.

q: Two hours after anterior cervical fusion, a patient develops neck swelling, stridor and agitation. What is the immediate action?
o: Open the wound to evacuate the haematoma and secure the airway
Sit up and give oxygen only
why: A neck haematoma can cause rapid airway obstruction; decompress immediately and secure the airway.

q: Which laryngoscopy approach minimises neck movement in a patient with cervical myelopathy?
o: Videolaryngoscope and bougie, with manual in-line stabilisation
LMA only for the whole case
why: Use a videolaryngoscope and bougie with manual in-line stabilisation; consider awake fibreoptic intubation for an unstable spine.

q: Why is TIVA preferred when neuromonitoring (MEPs) is used during spinal surgery?
o: Volatiles suppress evoked potentials more than propofol
why: Volatile agents, N2O, hypothermia and hypocapnia reduce signals; TIVA minimises interference. Avoid relaxant after intubation for MEPs.

q: In rheumatoid arthritis, what gap on a lateral C-spine X-ray indicates atlanto-axial subluxation?
o: Over 3 mm between the odontoid peg and the anterior arch of the atlas
why: A gap over 3 mm between the peg and the anterior arch of C1 suggests atlanto-axial subluxation and risk of cord compression.

q: Which airway feature of rheumatoid arthritis can cause stridor after extubation?
why: Cricoarytenoid arthritis can fix the cords; TMJ disease and cervical ankylosis also make the airway difficult.

q: From when after acute spinal cord injury is suxamethonium avoided because of hyperkalaemia?
o: Immediately at the time of injury
From around 72 hours to 6–18 months after injury
why: Extrajunctional receptors proliferate from about 72 hours, so avoid suxamethonium from then until 6–18 months.

q: A patient with a T4 complete spinal injury (injured 2 years ago) develops severe hypertension and flushing above the level during cystoscopy. What is happening?
why: Autonomic dysreflexia (injuries at or above T6) is an exaggerated sympathetic response to stimuli below the level. Remove the stimulus, deepen anaesthesia, then use vasodilators (GTN, nifedipine).

q: Which level of complete spinal cord injury causes diaphragmatic paralysis needing ventilation?
why: C3–5 supply the diaphragm. Injuries at or above C3 paralyse it; at or above T8 the intercostals are lost.
